findings.claim: Pre-war population of the Terezín garrison town prior to ghetto conversion (evacuated by July 1942)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Some summaries cite ~3,500–4,000 civilian residents alone; combined civilian (~3,700) plus military garrison (~3,500) totaled ~7,000–7,200 people. Civilian residents were completely expelled by July 1942.
sources: YIVO Encyclopedia / Yad Vashem / Academic refs: https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQEut4blehTEWPbXK2mONlKjYxOPhWsjJJKiF-wvFYlA3AF4puQL4SGPsFakjjp0ppOll2S-zP4CEXw4wnm_n3a8yagXcLBcBC0lTG9hBXiGOP_tk0uQkzIaJ8wS1DHUEL2nZYt8_qv-bg==

findings.claim: Footprint and physical area of the Terezín fortress town and designated ghetto space
findings.confidence: HIGH (fortress footprint); LOW CONFIDENCE (internal 335,056 m² / 95,000 m² split, single retrieved academic source)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: The walled octagonal Main Fortress (ghetto town) spans ~36 ha (0.36 km²) inside its ramparts, while the full 18th-century military fortress complex covers ~398 ha (~3.98 km²) and the modern municipality covers 13.52 km². Within the ghetto, Cambridge University Press cites 335,056 m² (~33.5 ha) total settlement space (42% built-up, 16% courtyards, 42% streets/gardens), with ~95,000 m² used as actual living quarters.
findings.value_or_range: 36 ha walled town (335,056 m² ghetto settlement; ~95,000 m² living quarters); 398 ha full fortress complex

findings.claim: Peak ghetto population reached in September 1942 (September 18, 1942; variant log date September 16, 1942)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Administrative logs cite 58,491 (with minor variant 58,497) on Sept 16 or Sept 18, 1942—more than 8 times the pre-war combined civilian-and-garrison population.

findings.claim: Average living space per prisoner at peak overcrowding (August–September 1942)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: H.G. Adler documents ~1.6 m² per inmate (including uninsulated attics and casemates); other summaries cite 1.5–2.0 m² or <2.5 m² depending on which auxiliary rooms/barracks are included.

findings.claim: Total Jewish prisoners sent to Terezín (November 1941–May 1945)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: ~140,000–141,184 covers regular ghetto transports (Nov 1941–Apr 1945); ~150,000–155,000 (Yad Vashem, Památník Terezín) adds the ~13,000–15,000 concentration camp evacuees forced into Terezín in April–May 1945.

findings.claim: Breakdown of regular ghetto arrivals (~140,000–141,184) by country/region of origin (1941–1945)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: The seven listed cohorts (Protectorate of Bohemia & Moravia 73,608; Germany 42,821 [var. 42,832]; Austria 15,266 [var. 15,254]; Netherlands 4,894 [var. 4,897]; Slovakia 1,447; Hungary 1,150; Denmark 476 [var. 466]) sum to 139,662; the remaining ~1,522 to reach 141,184 includes smaller groups (e.g., Bialystok children, unclassified arrivals) and ~207–230 births inside the ghetto.
findings.value_or_range: Bohemia & Moravia 73,608; Germany 42,821; Austria 15,266; Netherlands 4,894; Slovakia 1,447; Hungary 1,150; Denmark 476

findings.claim: Total deaths inside the Terezín ghetto itself (1941–1945)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: USHMM cites ~33,000 (rounded) and 33,456 (archival count of recorded ghetto deaths up to May 1945; variants 33,430–33,529). Yad Vashem cites ~35,000–35,440, which includes unregistered late-war evacuation deaths and ~1,500+ post-liberation deaths from the May–June 1945 typhus epidemic.
Occurred during peak overcrowding (~58,491 inmates), forcing rapid construction and operation of the ghetto crematorium in early September 1942.

findings.claim: Primary causes of death inside Terezín (digestive, respiratory, age-related, cardiac, infectious, and 1945 typhus)
findings.confidence: LOW CONFIDENCE (exact category counts from single retrieved scholarly source, Cambridge University Press / Adler)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Category counts derive from internal Jewish self-administration medical statistics (recorded diagnoses across select years) synthesized in H.G. Adler / Cambridge University Press; pulmonary tuberculosis was frequently co-diagnosed with cardiac failure, and the April–June 1945 typhus epidemic caused >2,190 hospital admissions, >500 pre-liberation deaths, and ~1,500 post-liberation deaths.
sources: Cambridge University Press (internal health reports & Adler): https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQGcq1y3dnct4K7hvWCcPVk3CgLnuvn5K_UtHpQ4kTCaLHWE42c1OUdWMWdXWFeDVw8TbchJSXPHnMjV-TM171u5MY6Tp0HOXJw5U0CvN5nBlV9u64cYcAa8NItF0-IRwzo4pB1IjW5CUCOM643bzuxyWRzVShN61XRY1UBJYyGzwxgfDmIWlbfXKV-10zu92CfXz34uR3IIDkeTKxED1mWZauLqbxo=
findings.value_or_range: Enteritis 8,664; age/senility 6,558; pneumonia 6,260; heart disease 3,473+; general infections 2,083+; typhus (spring 1945) >500 pre-liberation + ~1,500 post-liberation

findings.claim: Total deported east from Terezín (1942–1944, ~63 outward transports) and number of deportees who survived
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Total deported: ~87,000 (Auschwitz Museum) to 88,202 (USHMM) to ~90,000 (Yad Vashem). Survivors among those deported east: ~3,097–3,800 (~3.5%–4.3% survival rate; USHMM ~3,500, EHRI ~3,800).

findings.claim: Deportation breakdown by eastern destination (Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Maly Trostinets, Lublin district/Izbica/Zamość/Sobibor, Riga)
findings.confidence: MEDIUM (Auschwitz/Treblinka/Maly Trostinets/Lublin); LOW CONFIDENCE (Riga exact total from single source)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Auschwitz-Birkenau: 44,693–46,099; Treblinka: ~18,000 across 10 transports Bo–Bx in Sept–Oct 1942 (though some secondary summaries cite 8,000); Maly Trostinets: 5,000 across 5 transports (AAx, AAz, Bc, Bk, Bn of 1,000 each); Lublin district / Aktion Reinhard sites (Izbica Aa/Ab/Aq, Zamość Ar/As, Sobibor AAi at ~1,000 per transport); Riga: ~3,000 (transports O, P, Bb). Separately, ~1,200 Jews were sent to Switzerland in Feb 1945.
findings.value_or_range: Auschwitz 44,693–46,099; Treblinka ~18,000 (var. 8,000); Maly Trostinets 5,000; Izbica/Zamość/Sobibor 1,000+ per transport; Riga ~3,000

findings.claim: Prisoners liberated at Terezín in May 1945 (registered ghetto residents vs. total including April–May 1945 evacuees)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: 16,832 (USHMM, Cambridge, Yale) represents registered pre-evacuation ghetto residents at Soviet liberation on May 8–9, 1945; 17,247 reflects broader Red Cross / immediate post-liberation counts. Adding ~13,000–15,000 concentration-camp evacuees arriving in April–May 1945 brings the total liberated population to ~30,000.

findings.claim: Children in Terezín: popular '15,000 / ~100 survived' vs. modern archival counts (total under 15, deported, born in ghetto, died in ghetto, and liberated in May 1945)
findings.confidence: HIGH (1,633 liberated, 207–230 births, 7,590 deported, 142–245 deported survivors); LOW CONFIDENCE (~400 deaths inside Terezín from single retrieved medical-historical source)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Scholarly counts diverge for four key reasons: (1) The popular '~100' (archival 142, or up to 242–245 under broader age cutoffs) measures ONLY children deported east (out of 7,590 deported) who returned alive, ignoring the 1,633 children (<15) liberated inside Terezín in May 1945 (~half long-term residents never deported, ~half April–May 1945 evacuation arrivals); (2) Age cutoffs (<14 vs <15 vs <16/<18—~10,500–12,000 in strict under-15/regional cohorts vs ~15,000 under broader youth cutoffs); (3) Inclusion/exclusion of 207–230 births in Terezín (despite forced-abortion rules); (4) Inclusion/exclusion of late-war evacuation arrivals.
sources: Památník Terezín (7,590 deported, 142 deported survivors, ~1,600 liberated): https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFAtC__fCw9EBKpJwY0Es_gSUnDzjj4RKVDyqzF4dl3b7KtqGePFtEmTaxBFbv53nsjI31xR5Fix3dyx1zLGxyYQVJILY4MvUbqfxWBERR-O0WyO9TcB6YVZ98pmP3TT3l8xi82

findings.value_or_range: ~10,500–15,000 total; 7,590 deported east (142–245 survived); ~400 died in ghetto; 207–230 born; 1,633 (<15) liberated in Terezín

myths_checked: Popular claim '15,000 children passed through Terezín and only ~100 survived' (from early postwar accounts such as Hana Volavková's 'I Never Saw Another Butterfly'): Checked against Památník Terezín, Terezín Initiative, Miroslav Kárný, and Anna Hájková (Cambridge University Press). The ~100 figure (more precisely 142, or up to 242–245 depending on age cutoff) reflects only children deported east (out of ~7,590 deported) who returned alive; it omits the 1,633 children (<15) who survived inside Terezín until May 1945 liberation (roughly half pre-evacuation ghetto children, half late-war evacuation arrivals). Furthermore, strict under-15 cohorts yield ~10,500–12,000 children rather than 15,000 (which reflects broader youth cutoffs up to 16–18).

Claim that '8,000' prisoners were deported to Treblinka vs. full transport roster: Checked against Yad Vashem Transports to Extinction and Terezín Initiative Institute (terezinstudies.cz), which document 10 consecutive transports (Bo through Bx, Sept 19–Oct 22, 1942) to Treblinka totaling ~18,000 deportees.

Claim that '16,832' or '17,247' represents all prisoners liberated at Terezín in May 1945: Checked against USHMM and Cambridge University Press; 16,832–17,247 counts registered pre-evacuation ghetto survivors only, whereas adding ~13,000–15,000 concentration-camp evacuees arriving in April–May 1945 yields ~30,000 total prisoners liberated.
